title: Pollution
tagline: Air, water, soil and noise pollution: their sources, their effects and the means of control

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class IX Geography unit 'Pollution'. The unit prescribes the types of pollution - air, water (fresh and marine), soil, radiation and noise - together with their sources, their effects on the environment and on human health, and their preventive measures, and this chapter follows that structure. The sources named are the standard ones for the unit: vehicular, industrial and the burning of garbage for air; domestic and industrial waste for water; chemical fertilisers, biomedical waste and pesticides for soil; X-rays and the radioactive fallout of nuclear plants for radiation; and traffic, factories, construction sites, loudspeakers and airports for noise. No specific local case study is prescribed by the syllabus and none is presented as such. No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

learningOutcomes: Define pollution and distinguish between the main types of pollution.
State the sources, the effects and the control measures of air, water, soil, radiation and noise pollution.
Explain eutrophication and the effect of noise pollution on human health.
Describe the methods of solid waste management and the three Rs.
State what individuals, communities and governments can each do to reduce pollution.

overview.intro: Pollution is any undesirable change in the environment that harms living organisms, and the types studied here are air, water, soil, radiation and noise pollution. Air pollution comes mainly from the burning of fossil fuels and from the burning of garbage, so it is worst where coal is burnt in industry and in power stations and where there are many vehicles on the roads; some pollutants are released as they are, and others are formed in the air by chemical reactions, as in photochemical smog and acid rain. Water pollution comes from domestic and industrial waste, from agricultural runoff and from oil, in the rivers and lakes and in the sea as well, and the most serious effect of nutrient pollution is eutrophication, in which algae flourish, die and are decomposed by bacteria that use up the dissolved oxygen, so the fish die. Soil pollution is largely the result of chemical fertilisers, pesticides and biomedical waste, and of the careless dumping of waste. Radiation pollution comes from the use of X-rays and from the radioactive fallout of nuclear plants. Noise pollution is the most complained of form in cities. All of them are curable, and the measures that work fall into three groups: stopping the pollutant at the source, treating it before it reaches the environment, and managing the waste properly in the first place, which is where the three Rs, reduce, reuse and recycle, come in.

facts.label: Main air pollutants

facts.label: Types of pollution
facts.value: Air, water (fresh and marine), soil, radiation and noise

blocks.text: Air pollution is the presence in the air of substances that harm living things. Pollutants released directly into the air are called primary pollutants, and the chief of them are particulate matter, such as dust, soot and ash, sulphur dioxide from the burning of coal and oil, oxides of nitrogen from high-temperature combustion, carbon monoxide from the incomplete burning of fuels, lead from petrol and from smelters, and hydrocarbons from the burning of oil. Secondary pollutants are formed in the air itself by chemical reactions between primary pollutants and sunlight. The two most important of these are photochemical smog, which forms in the sunlight over a city and includes a mixture of ozone, oxides of nitrogen and aldehydes, and acid rain, which is produced when oxides of sulphur and nitrogen combine with water vapour in the air to form sulphuric and nitric acids.

blocks.caption: Table: sources, effects and control of air pollution
rows: Sources
Factories and power stations burning coal and oil, motor vehicles, brick kilns, household smoke and firewood, the open burning of garbage, and the burning of crop stubble in the fields
Effects on health
Irritation of the eyes, throat and nose, bronchitis and asthma, breathlessness, and a higher risk of lung disease; children and the elderly suffer most
Effects on the environment
Acid rain, photochemical smog, reduced visibility, damage to crops and to buildings and monuments, and the greenhouse effect
Control at the source
Use of cleaner fuels, lead-free petrol, catalytic converters in vehicles, and better combustion practice in boilers
Control before release
Electrostatic precipitators, scrubbers and cyclone separators in factories, and chimneys tall enough to disperse the smoke
Control on the ground
Planting of green belts around factories, public transport, and the control of stubble burning

items: The smoke and gases of a factory chimney should be released high above the ground so that they are dispersed before they reach the people below.
An electrostatic precipitator removes fine dust by giving the particles an electric charge and drawing them to collecting plates.
A scrubber washes the gases of a flue with water or a chemical solution to remove the harmful gases.
The catalytic converter of a car changes carbon monoxide, oxides of nitrogen and hydrocarbons into less harmful gases, and it works properly only if lead-free petrol is used.
Green belts of trees around factories filter dust, absorb carbon dioxide and reduce noise, but they cannot remove the whole of the pollution.

blocks.text: Water is polluted when substances that are harmful or unusable are added to it. The chief sources are domestic sewage from towns and cities, industrial effluent from factories, agricultural runoff carrying fertilisers and pesticides from the fields, thermal pollution from the hot water discharged by power stations and factories, and oil spills from tankers and from offshore drilling. The most damaging of these for lakes and rivers is the nutrient enrichment of the water by fertilisers and by untreated sewage, which produces eutrophication. In this process the nutrients, mainly nitrates and phosphates, cause a rapid growth of algae on the surface; the algae die, and bacteria that decompose them use up the dissolved oxygen; with the oxygen exhausted, the fish and other aquatic animals suffocate, and a dead zone is created.

items.meaning: The wastewater of a town, carrying human waste, wash water and factory effluent into the drains.
The liquid waste discharged from a factory or a treatment plant.
The enrichment of water with nutrients, leading to algal growth, the depletion of dissolved oxygen and the death of aquatic life.
The build-up of a substance such as mercury in the tissues of an organism, which becomes more concentrated at each step of the food chain.
The heating of river or lake water by the hot effluent of power stations and factories, which reduces the dissolved oxygen and kills fish.

items: Untreated sewage carries the bacteria of cholera, typhoid and dysentery, so the treatment of sewage is a public health measure and not only an environmental one.
Industrial effluent may contain acids, alkalis, dyes, detergents, oils and heavy metals such as lead, mercury and cadmium.
Excess fertilisers wash off the fields into rivers and lakes and, together with sewage, cause eutrophication.
Sewage treatment plants remove the solids by screening and settling, the organic matter by bacterial digestion in filter beds, and the pathogens by chlorination before the water is released.
Rainwater harvesting, the re-use of treated wastewater for irrigation and industry, and the treatment of every settlement's sewage at a plant are the practical measures.

blocks.text: Soil is polluted mainly by the careless use of chemical fertilisers and pesticides, by the dumping of solid and industrial waste, by the discharge of industrial effluent onto the land, and by the disposal of radioactive waste. The effect is a fall in the fertility of the soil, a fall in the yield of the crops, the contamination of the food grown on it, and the contamination of the groundwater beneath. Noise pollution is the unwanted sound of sufficient intensity to disturb the people who hear it, and its sources in a city are motor vehicles, horns and loudspeakers, factories and their machinery, construction work, generators and pumps, and air conditioners. The effects on health are hearing impairment, sleeplessness, irritability, loss of concentration and raised blood pressure, and children and old people are especially affected.

blocks.caption: Table: soil and noise pollution compared
rows: Main sources
Chemical fertilisers, pesticides and biomedical waste, industrial and solid waste, effluent discharged on land
Traffic, horns and loudspeakers, factories and their machinery, construction sites, airports and aircraft, generators and air conditioners
Effects
Loss of soil fertility, lower crop yield, contaminated food and groundwater, bioaccumulation of poisons
Hearing impairment, sleeplessness, stress, poor concentration and raised blood pressure
Control
Organic farming, vermicomposting, biofertilisers, crop rotation, proper disposal of industrial waste
Silencers and sound absorbers, zoning of industrial areas, restriction of horns and loudspeakers, green belts as noise barriers

items: Vermicomposting uses earthworms to break down organic waste into a rich compost, and it disposes of the waste and improves the soil at the same time.
Biofertilisers such as rhizobium and mycorrhiza help the plants to draw more nutrients from the soil, so less chemical fertiliser is needed.
Crop rotation with a legume restores the nitrogen of the soil naturally.
The noise level is measured in decibels, and the permissible limits are set by law for different zones, with the strictest limits in residential and hospital areas.
Green belts of trees act as noise barriers because the foliage absorbs and scatters the sound.

blocks.text: Radiation pollution is the contamination of the environment by radiation that is released beyond the place where it is safe to release it. Its sources are the X-rays and the other forms of radiation used in medicine and in industry, and the radioactive fallout from nuclear plants and from nuclear tests. The materials that produce the radiation are called radioactive materials, and they continue to give out radiation for as long as they remain radioactive. Radiation is invisible, it is felt only through its effects, and it can harm the body of a person who is exposed to it for a long time, causing burns, the destruction of the blood-forming tissues, and in severe cases the shortening of life and the death of the cell. When the radioactive material reaches the food chain it is taken up by the plants and the animals and reaches the human body, and in the case of the long-lived isotopes the damage may continue to show in the children of those who were exposed.

items: The dose of radiation that a person receives is measured in millisieverts, and the medical use of X-rays is controlled so that the dose to the patient stays within safe limits.
The material that has been used in medicine and industry should be returned to the supplier and disposed of by the proper agency, and it must never be thrown into ordinary waste or into a water body.
A nuclear plant has thick walls of concrete and lead to contain the radiation, and the surrounding area is monitored continuously by the authorities.
Radioactive waste should be sealed in containers and stored in safe places far from human settlements, and it should be monitored for a long period.

learn.title: Waste management, the three Rs and community action

blocks.text: Solid waste in a city comes from houses, shops, factories and hospitals, and it must be collected and disposed of. The simplest method is the sanitary landfill, in which the waste is compacted and covered with soil, but it uses land, it produces leachate that can pollute the groundwater, and it gives off methane, which is a greenhouse gas. Composting, and vermicomposting in particular, turns the biodegradable part of the waste into a useful soil conditioner. Incineration reduces the volume of the waste and can generate energy, but it is expensive and it releases some harmful gases unless the plant is well controlled. Recycling keeps materials such as paper, glass, metals and plastics in use and saves raw materials and energy. The order in which these should be applied is the waste hierarchy, and the three Rs, reduce, reuse and recycle, sit at the heart of it.

items.meaning: To cut the amount of waste produced in the first place, by buying only what is needed and by avoiding disposable and over-packaged goods.
To use a product again for the same or a different purpose before discarding it, such as using a cloth bag for shopping or a jar for storage.
To process a waste material into a new product, such as old paper into new paper or waste plastic into new plastic.
A plant in which the biodegradable part of the waste is decomposed in the absence of air to produce combustible gas and manure.
The practice of keeping wastes such as wet waste, dry waste and hazardous waste in separate bins at the place where they are made.

items: Segregation of waste at source into wet, dry and hazardous waste makes the rest of the system work, because mixed waste cannot be recycled or composted.
Biodegradable waste should be composted or used in a biogas plant, and it should never go to a landfill, where it rots and produces methane.
Hazardous waste from hospitals and from batteries should be collected separately and given to authorised handlers.

A community can act through waste segregation, composting of kitchen waste, the reuse of cloth and containers, the repair of articles instead of replacing them, and by putting pressure on local authorities for collection and processing facilities.
The responsibility is shared: individuals reduce and segregate, industries treat their own effluent and emissions, and governments set the standards and provide the facilities.

figures.caption: Figure: Sources of air pollution and how they are controlled
figures.description: Primary pollutants leave the chimney or the exhaust pipe directly, while secondary pollutants such as smog and acid rain are formed in the air by the action of sunlight on those primary pollutants. Control is applied at the source, before release and on the ground.

figures.caption: Figure: Eutrophication in a lake
figures.description: Fertilisers and sewage raise the nutrient content of the water, algae grow rapidly, the algae die, and the bacteria that decompose them use up the dissolved oxygen. Fish then suffocate and a dead zone forms on the lake bed.

keyPoints: Pollution is any undesirable change in the environment that harms living organisms.
Air pollution is of two kinds: primary pollutants released directly and secondary pollutants formed in the air.
The chief primary air pollutants are particulate matter, sulphur dioxide, oxides of nitrogen, carbon monoxide, lead and hydrocarbons.
Photochemical smog and acid rain are secondary pollutants.
Air pollution is controlled at the source, before release through chimneys and scrubbers, and on the ground by green belts.
The catalytic converter of a vehicle reduces carbon monoxide, oxides of nitrogen and hydrocarbons.
Water pollution comes from sewage, industrial effluent, agricultural runoff, thermal discharge and oil spills.
Eutrophication is caused by nutrients, produces an algal bloom, depletes the dissolved oxygen and kills fish.
Sewage treatment, effluent treatment and the re-use of treated water are the main controls of water pollution.
Soil pollution is caused by chemicals, waste dumping and effluent on land, and is controlled by organic farming, vermicomposting and biofertilisers.
Radiation pollution comes from X-rays and from the radioactive fallout of nuclear plants, and it is controlled by shielding, safe disposal and long-term monitoring of radioactive waste.
Noise pollution affects hearing, sleep and mental health, and is controlled by silencers, zoning and restrictions on horns and loudspeakers.
The three Rs are reduce, reuse and recycle, and segregation at source is the first step in all three.
Waste is disposed of by landfill, composting, incineration and recycling, and the order of preference is the waste hierarchy.
examFocus: Comparison questions are the commonest form in this unit, so prepare a table for each pair: air and water, soil and noise, or the sources, effects and control of one type.
A question on a source of pollution usually wants the mechanism as well as the source, for example that burning coal in a power station releases sulphur dioxide.
For the control measures, group them as technical, such as scrubbers and catalytic converters, and as personal or administrative, such as public transport and zoning, and explain one of them.
Questions on the three Rs expect the meaning of each R with an example from daily life, so keep a personal example ready.
For the health effects, name the specific ailment, such as bronchitis, asthma or hearing impairment, rather than writing that it affects health in general.

vocabulary.meaning: Any undesirable change in the environment that harms living organisms.
A pollutant released directly into the air, such as particulate matter or sulphur dioxide.
A pollutant formed in the air by chemical reactions, such as photochemical smog or acid rain.
The enrichment of water with nutrients, leading to algal growth and the depletion of oxygen.
The build-up of a substance in the tissues of an organism along a food chain.
A device that washes flue gases with water or a chemical solution to remove harmful gases.
A device in a vehicle that converts harmful exhaust gases into less harmful ones.
The making of compost with the help of earthworms.
Keeping different kinds of waste separate at the place where they are produced.
Material that gives out radiation and that must be sealed, stored and monitored for a long period.
Radioactive material that settles from the air after a nuclear test or an accident at a nuclear plant.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a secondary air pollutant?
questions.explanation: Photochemical smog is formed in the air by the action of sunlight on oxides of nitrogen and hydrocarbons, so it is a secondary pollutant. Sulphur dioxide, particulate matter and carbon monoxide are released directly and are primary pollutants.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing particulate matter, which is a primary pollutant even though it is often the most harmful of the direct emissions.

questions.prompt: The enrichment of lake water with nutrients, leading to algal growth and the death of fish, is called:
questions.explanation: Eutrophication is the enrichment of water with nitrates and phosphates, which causes an algal bloom, and the decay of the algae then uses up the dissolved oxygen and kills the fish.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing thermal pollution, which is the heating of the water by hot industrial discharge.

questions.prompt: The device fitted in a vehicle that converts harmful exhaust gases into less harmful ones is the:
questions.explanation: The catalytic converter changes carbon monoxide, oxides of nitrogen and hydrocarbons into carbon dioxide, nitrogen and water, and it works only with lead-free petrol. The electrostatic precipitator and the scrubber are factory devices.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing the scrubber, which cleans the flue gases of a factory and not the exhaust of a car.

questions.prompt: The practice of keeping wet waste, dry waste and hazardous waste in separate bins at the place where they are produced is called:
questions.explanation: Segregation at source is the first step of waste management, because mixed waste cannot be composted or recycled and the different fractions have to be separated before they are collected.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing incineration, which is a method of disposal rather than a method of sorting.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following is a method of disposing of waste that recovers a useful material?
questions.explanation: Recycling processes waste such as paper, glass, metal and plastic into new products, so it saves raw materials and energy and keeps the material out of the landfill. Open dumping and open burning are themselves sources of pollution.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing open burning, which is a source of air pollution rather than a method of recovering material.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the three Rs of waste management are reduce, ______ and recycle.
questions.explanation: The three Rs are reduce, reuse and recycle, in that order of preference. Reduce means making less waste, reuse means using a product again, and recycle means making a new product from the waste.
questions.commonMistake: Answering 'recycle' again, which repeats a word and loses the sequence.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the waste of hospitals, batteries and other hazardous material must be collected separately and given to ________ handlers.
questions.explanation: Hazardous waste is handled by authorised agencies under separate rules, because it can contaminate the soil and groundwater and can poison people who come into contact with it.
questions.commonMistake: Leaving the blank with 'the municipal' or 'any', which would defeat the point of separate collection.

questions.prompt: Explain the process of eutrophication and state two effects of it on a lake.
questions.answer: Fertilisers washed off the fields and the phosphates in untreated sewage raise the nutrient content of the lake water. The nutrients cause a rapid growth of algae, which forms a green bloom on the surface of the water and prevents light from reaching the deeper water. When the algae die they are decomposed by bacteria, and this decomposition uses up the dissolved oxygen of the water. With the oxygen exhausted, a dead zone forms on the lake bed, the fish suffocate and die, and the lake may also develop an unpleasant smell as the organic matter decays. Among the effects of the process are the death of fish and other aquatic animals, the loss of the lake as a source of fish for the local people, the fouling of the water with floating algae and odour, and the reduction of the recreation value of the lake.
questions.explanation: The sequence of nutrient enrichment, algal bloom, decay, oxygen depletion and death is the whole explanation, and the effects must follow from it.
questions.commonMistake: Stopping at the algal bloom, without explaining that the oxygen is used up in the decomposition of the dead algae.

questions.prompt: State four ways in which individuals can reduce the pollution they cause.
questions.answer: Use public transport, a bicycle or a shared vehicle instead of a private car whenever the journey allows, so that the exhaust of many vehicles is avoided. Carry a cloth bag for shopping and a refillable bottle for water, and refuse plastic bags and packaged food, which add to the waste that has to be disposed of. Segregate the waste at home into wet, dry and hazardous waste, and compost the kitchen waste in a compost pit or a bin. Dispose of the waste of batteries, medicines and electronic goods through the authorised collection system rather than in the municipal bin, and never burn leaves or stubble in the open. Use bulbs, fans and appliances of good energy efficiency, and close the taps while brushing the teeth, so that less energy and water are used.
questions.explanation: Each measure has to be practical and connected to a particular type of pollution.
questions.commonMistake: Repeating the same idea in different words instead of giving four distinct actions.

questions.prompt: Explain how the control of air pollution in industry differs from the control of air pollution from vehicles.
questions.answer: The sources are different and so are the controls. A factory releases its pollution through tall chimneys in large volumes, so the controls act on the flue gases before they leave: an electrostatic precipitator removes the fine particles of dust, a scrubber washes the harmful gases out of the smoke, and the chimney is made tall enough that the gases are dispersed in the upper air before they can reach the people below. The factory is also kept away from residential areas by zoning, and trees are planted around it. A vehicle, on the other hand, produces a small volume of pollution but does so at the level of the street, right where people walk and breathe, so the control is applied to the fuel and to the exhaust of each vehicle: the catalytic converter changes the harmful exhaust gases, lead-free petrol is used so that the converter is not poisoned, and the level of emission is checked by the pollution under control certificate. In both cases the source is the target, but the technical means and the scale of the operation are different.
questions.explanation: A good comparison sets out the difference in the source and then matches a control measure to each.
questions.commonMistake: Giving the same two measures for both, without showing that they act on different sources.

questions.prompt: Describe the methods of managing solid waste in a city, setting out the advantages and disadvantages of each, and explain the place of the three Rs in the scheme.
questions.answer: The first step in the management of solid waste is segregation at source, in which households and offices keep wet, dry and hazardous waste in separate bins, because the different fractions have to be separated before anything can be done with them. The methods of disposal then differ. In a sanitary landfill the waste is compacted, covered with soil and monitored; it is cheap and it handles large quantities, but it uses valuable land, it produces leachate that can pollute the groundwater, and it gives off methane, which adds to the greenhouse effect. In composting, and vermicomposting in particular, the biodegradable waste is decomposed by bacteria or by earthworms into a rich soil conditioner; this removes the waste from the city and improves the soil, but it can be done only where there is space and it cannot deal with the non-biodegradable fraction. Incineration burns the waste in a controlled furnace, which reduces its volume greatly and can generate energy for the city, but it is expensive, it needs a modern plant, and it releases some harmful gases unless the emissions are cleaned. Recycling processes materials such as paper, glass, metals and plastics into new products; it saves raw materials and energy and creates employment, but it works only if the waste has already been segregated and if there is a market for the recycled material. The three Rs, reduce, reuse and recycle, sit above all these methods in the waste hierarchy, because the cheapest and cleanest treatment of waste is not to make it in the first place. Reduce means buying only what is needed and avoiding disposable and over-packaged goods, reuse means using an article again before discarding it, and recycle means sending the material to be made into something new. The order matters, because a tonne of waste that is never created costs nothing to dispose of, while a tonne that is created has to be collected, transported and treated.
questions.explanation: Each method needs its advantages and its disadvantages, and the three Rs have to be placed above the methods rather than treated as one more method.
questions.commonMistake: Describing only the methods of disposal without the segregation that makes them possible, or treating the three Rs as a fourth method of disposal.

questions.prompt: Explain what soil pollution is, describe its main sources and effects, and suggest the measures by which it can be reduced.
questions.answer: Soil pollution means the presence in the soil of substances that harm the soil itself, the crops grown on it or the people who eat them. The chief sources are the excessive and careless use of chemical fertilisers and pesticides, which destroy the useful organisms of the soil and upset its balance, and leave residues in the crop; the dumping of solid waste and of industrial waste on open ground, which adds heavy metals to the soil; the discharge of industrial effluent onto land rather than into a treatment plant; the disposal of radioactive waste; and the excessive use of fertilisers combined with soil erosion, which leaves the land exhausted. The effects are a steady loss of soil fertility and of the organic content of the soil, a fall in the yield of the crops, the contamination of the food that is grown on the land and of the groundwater beneath it, and the build-up of poisons in the bodies of people and animals through the food chain. The measures are to reduce and to control. Organic farming, in which chemical fertilisers are replaced by manure, compost and biofertilisers such as rhizobium and mycorrhiza, restores the life of the soil and cuts the residue in the crop. Crop rotation with a legume restores the nitrogen naturally. Vermicomposting turns the organic waste of the city into a soil conditioner and disposes of that waste at the same time. Industrial waste must be treated and disposed of by the methods laid down by law, and not tipped on open land, and hazardous waste must go to authorised handlers. Afforestation and the protection of the vegetative cover check the erosion that carries the topsoil away. Finally, the soil must be tested regularly, so that the contamination that does occur is detected early.
questions.explanation: The answer needs sources with their mechanism, effects on the soil, the crop and the body, and measures that are matched to those sources.
questions.commonMistake: Mentioning only the visible effect on the crop and forgetting the groundwater and the food chain, which are the more serious effects.

questions.prompt: Examine the claim that pollution is only a problem caused by large industries, and show why it is not.
questions.answer: The claim is convenient for the industries and wrong on the evidence. Industry is only one of the sources, and in many towns it is not even the largest. Every motor vehicle that is used and every kilometre that is driven adds exhaust gases and fine particles to the air, and the exhaust of a single badly maintained vehicle can pollute the air around it far more than any one factory does; a city with a million vehicles may deal with more pollutant in total than the factories of the whole region. The burning of firewood, coal and cow dung in the homes of a large part of the population adds smoke, carbon monoxide and particles, and the open burning of the stubble of the fields adds smoke that is carried over whole districts. Domestic sewage from every household, if it is not treated, is a continuous source of water pollution, and the domestic waste of every household is the largest single component of the waste that a city has to dispose of. On the soil, the misuse of fertilisers and pesticides by farmers and the dumping of waste by households have nothing to do with factories at all. Noise pollution is almost entirely a product of traffic, horns, construction and domestic appliances. The point of a fair analysis is therefore that the sources are many and are shared, and this matters for the solution as much as for the diagnosis, because a remedy that leaves out the household and the vehicle misses most of the pollution. That is the argument for public transport, for cleaner household fuels, for segregation at source and for the three Rs, and against the idea that the problem will disappear if the factory is closed. What is true is that industry is usually the most visible and the most easily measured source, and that it is often concentrated, which is why it can be regulated effectively; that is a different argument from the one being examined here.
questions.explanation: The answer must take the claim seriously, list the sources that are not industrial with their scale, and then draw the conclusion about policy rather than only about causes.
questions.commonMistake: Simply saying that household and vehicle pollution is small, which is not true and is easily contradicted by the scale of city traffic.
